metadata.title: The Cash Machine The Market Put On Sale: INTU

content.text:
The market is selling shares in a software giant as if its cash-generating days are numbered, yet the business is paying out more than double the average company.
Intuit (INTU), the company behind TurboTax and QuickBooks, currently trades around $289.92 a share, a level that reflects a steep decline of 28% over the last three months. Yet for every dollar an investor parks in the stock, the business hands back 9.6% in annual free cash. That free cash flow yield is more than double the 4.1% paid by the median S&P 500 company. The market is offering premium cash flow at a discount price. The question is whether this is a genuine bargain on a durable machine, or if the market is correctly pricing in a future breakdown.
So where is all this cash coming from?
This level of profitability is not a recent fluke. Intuit's operating margin over the last twelve months was 28%, comfortably above its three-year average of 26%. The cash is generated by its core software businesses, which serve millions of consumers and small businesses. While the company is a mature software provider, it has found powerful new sources of expansion. Management recently highlighted that its key growth areas, assisted tax, its money portfolio, and mid-market, are all expanding at a rapid clip, with each segment "growing north of 30%."
The most significant driver is the strategic shift toward human-assisted services. The company's TurboTax Live offering, which connects filers with tax experts, is a standout. Management expects TurboTax Live revenue to grow 36% this year. This single service is on track to represent 53% of total TurboTax revenue, a testament to a successful pivot into higher-value services. Some analysis suggests certain stocks can be priced like a decline but paying like a machine, and Intuit's numbers seem to fit that description.
Why would the market discount a business with these growth engines?
For the market to be right, the cash flow has to be at risk. The primary concern centers on the company's original Do-It-Yourself (DIY) tax business. Management is "constructively dissatisfied" with its performance in this segment, admitting that among the most price-sensitive filers, "We lost on price." This isn't a new issue, and it creates a drag on the overall consumer story. The problem is compounded by a broader market contraction, as total IRS filers are expected to decline by approximately 30-basis-points this season.
There is also a drag from a past acquisition. Revenue from Mailchimp was "down slightly versus a year ago," prompting the company to rightsize its investment in the unit. The market's apprehension is that the pricing pressure in the core DIY segment and the underperformance of Mailchimp are persistent problems that could erode the impressive gains being made elsewhere.
